note: Revised data set for theology-compass.html after the twenty-lens fairness audit (522 findings; 424 survived a three-lens accuracy/fairness/necessity verification), plus a repair pass that re-derived the tradition coordinates from the eighteen published answer sheets in `simulations`. Scores run 0..100 per axis: 0 = left pole, 100 = right pole. `scoring` describes what theology-compass.html actually computes today; `scoring_v1_proposed` holds the rules the audit specified that are NOT in the page and that apply.js cannot add. Applying this file alone does not close the blockers listed there. Every change is itemised in the changelog array, each entry carrying a status of 'applied to data' or 'specified, not yet in code'; kept findings deliberately not applied are in the disputed array.

scoring.statement_direction: +1 means agreeing pushes toward the RIGHT pole of the axis, -1 toward the LEFT pole
scoring.axis_raw: sum over the three statements of (direction * response), range -6..+6
scoring.axis_score: round((raw + 6) / 12 * 100), so 0 = fully left pole, 50 = center, 100 = fully right pole
scoring.headline: take the three axes with the largest |score - 50|, join their band adjectives; if all six are within 10 of 50, label is "A theological centrist"
scoring.nearest_tradition: Euclidean distance in the six-dimensional 0..100 space to each tradition position; the two smallest are shown as "Closest traditions"; match % = round(100 - distance / sqrt(6 * 100^2) * 100)

scoring_v1_proposed.status: SPECIFIED, NOT IMPLEMENTED. theology-compass.html runs the rules in `scoring` above; nothing here is in the page. Each item below is also a changelog entry whose target begins 'scoring:' or 'page copy / code'. Publishing the data file without these code edits ships a page whose behaviour contradicts this file, so the rules were moved here rather than left in `scoring`.
scoring_v1_proposed.headline: candidates are the axes whose band is not the middle band, ordered by |score - 50| descending, ties broken by the number of Strongly answers on that axis and then by axis order; take at most three and join their band adjectives. No candidates -> 'Near the center on every axis'; one or two candidates -> those adjectives alone. (survey-23; blocked: the page's headline() still includes middle bands, so the neutral midpoint bands print as convictions.)
scoring_v1_proposed.nearest_tradition: Euclidean distance in the six-dimensional 0..100 space to each tradition position; the two smallest are shown as 'Nearest on the map'. match % = round(100 - distance / 198 * 100), 198 being the largest distance between any two listed traditions after the repair pass (Eastern Orthodox to Bible church, 198.1). If the two nearest are within 10 units of each other, show them as jointly nearest rather than ranked; if the nearest is more than 45 units away, read 'No listed tradition is a close fit. Nearest, loosely: X, Y'; if all six axes are within 10 of 50, name no tradition at all. (mockery-15, survey-24, wesleyan-1.)
scoring_v1_proposed.hedge_calibration: The 45-unit threshold is derived from the eighteen sheets in `simulations`: an informed adherent scored through the eighteen statements lands 9.1 to 25.5 units from their own entry (median 15.7), so 45 is about 1.8x the worst informed-adherent distance. The earlier 60-unit figure was set by eye. Note that 89% of the 4,826,809 reachable score vectors lie more than 45 units from every entry, and 71% lie more than 60 units away; that is a fact about a mostly empty six-dimensional space, not a defect, but it means the hedge is the normal case for answer sets no tradition holds.
scoring_v1_proposed.all_central_suppression: When every axis is within 10 of 50, print no tradition at all. This is the only fix for wesleyan-1: after the repair pass the entry nearest the all-Unsure point [50,50,50,50,50,50] is Mainline Protestant at 67.1 units (73% on the page's shipped denominator), with Wesleyan at 72.7 and Anglican at 73.1. No honest coordinate for a broad, centrally placed tradition is further out than that, so the blocker cannot be closed in the data alone.
scoring_v1_proposed.permalink: each axis stored as round(score * 12 / 100) (0..12), packed base 13, rendered base 36 and left-padded to six characters, so every reachable score round-trips exactly. The page still stores round(score/4) in base 32, so nine of the thirteen reachable scores reopen as a different value (copy-7, survey-22).

axes.name: Grace
axes.fair_summary: Monergists (God alone brings a person to faith) hold that salvation is God's work from beginning to end: God chooses his people, calls them, and works faith in them; the sinner contributes nothing to conversion, not even the decision to believe. Monergists differ on whether that grace can be resisted: the Reformed hold that it makes the unwilling willing and cannot finally be refused, and that God keeps his people to the end; Lutherans hold that it can be refused, even to the end, so that the lost are lost by their own resistance and not by God's decree. Synergists (the person freely cooperates with the grace God gives) hold that God's grace always comes first and makes faith possible, but that each person must freely respond and can decline, so that election follows God's foreknowledge of faith or rests on his choice of a people in Christ. Many synergists, including most Baptists, nonetheless hold that God keeps every true believer to the end. Protestants on this side usually call themselves Arminian or Wesleyan; the Christian East speaks of synergy. One caution about how this axis is built: statement 2 scores resistible grace toward the synergist pole, because resistibility is the question that separates the Reformed from every other tradition on the map. A confessional Lutheran who answers his own confession honestly therefore lands in the monergist-leaning band rather than at the pole; that is a deliberate cost of a three-item axis, not a verdict on his monergism. A four-item version separates the two questions (see candidate_statements).

history.what: Augustine argues against Pelagius that grace must precede and enable every good will.
John Cassian, Conferences XIII, teaches that grace and free will cooperate at every step; the Christian East still calls this synergy.
Second Council of Orange: even the beginning of faith is God's gift, yet it condemns any predestination to evil and says the baptized can, with Christ's help, do what salvation requires.
Luther, The Bondage of the Will, answers Erasmus's defense of free choice.
Council of Trent, Decree on Justification: grace comes first and enables, yet the will freely cooperates and can refuse.
Formula of Concord (arts. II, XI): conversion is God's work alone, yet grace can be resisted and no one is predestined to damnation.
The Remonstrance sets out five Arminian articles; the Synod of Dort replies with five points.
Synod of Jerusalem condemns the Calvinist confession published under Patriarch Cyril Lucaris's name: God predestines according to his foreknowledge of each person's free use of the will.
Wesley's sermon Free Grace and Whitefield's printed reply divide the evangelical revival over predestination.

left: Luther, The Bondage of the Will
right: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition II.29–30

axes.name: Table
axes.fair_summary: The sacramental view holds that God really gives grace through the sacraments: Christ is truly present in the Supper, and baptism is a means by which God joins a person to Christ and his church; most churches on this side also baptize infants, whether as children of the covenant or for the washing of new birth. The memorial view holds that the Supper is a remembrance and proclamation of Christ's death until he comes, and baptism a believer's public confession of faith, so both are ordinances that believers keep in obedience rather than channels of grace: whatever blessing comes with them comes by the faith of those who take part, not through the elements themselves. Many stand between the poles, baptizing believers only while holding that Christ spiritually feeds his people at the Table (Reformed Baptists) or that God forgives sins in baptism (Churches of Christ).

history.what: Ignatius of Antioch calls the Eucharist the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ.
John of Damascus, Exact Exposition IV.13: the bread and wine are changed into Christ's body and blood by the invocation and presence of the Holy Spirit, 'not merely figures'.
Fourth Lateran Council affirms transubstantiation in its profession of faith; Trent defines it in 1551.
Zwingli argues that 'is' in 'this is my body' means 'signifies': the Supper is a memorial of thanksgiving.
First believers' baptisms in Zurich begin the Anabaptist movement; the Schleitheim Confession sets out believers' baptism and a memorial Supper.
Marburg Colloquy: Luther and Zwingli agree on fourteen of fifteen articles but not on whether Christ's body is bodily present in the bread and wine: Luther affirms, Zwingli denies.
Calvin's final Institutes (IV.17): a real spiritual presence, received by faith through the Spirit.

English Baptists, out of Separatism rather than Anabaptism: John Smyth's Amsterdam congregation baptizes believers, and the Particular Baptists' London Confessions specify immersion and confess Christ 'spiritually present to the faith of believers' at the Supper.

left: Schmemann, For the Life of the World
right: Hubmaier, On the Christian Baptism of Believers

axes.name: Gifts
bands: open but cautious on the gifts
axes.fair_summary: Continuationists hold that the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy, and healing, remain available to the church until Christ returns and are to be welcomed and tested, though they differ on how eagerly to seek them: Pentecostals and charismatics seek them openly, while Catholic and Orthodox teaching receives them with gratitude and warns against seeking them rashly. Cessationists hold that those sign gifts authenticated the apostles and their message and passed away once the apostolic foundation was laid; many add that the completed Scriptures now do the work those gifts once did. They affirm that God still heals and answers prayer, but hold that the Spirit's ordinary work is now through the Word and providence rather than through the sign gifts.

history.what: Irenaeus (Against Heresies II.32; V.6) reports prophecy, tongues, and healings in the churches; Montanist 'new prophecy' in Phrygia leaves the wider church wary of prophetic claims.
Chrysostom, Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians, says the gifts Paul lists there 'used to occur but now no longer take place'.
Augustine, City of God XXII.8, records recent miracles at Hippo, many at martyrs' shrines, and in his Retractations withdraws his earlier claim that miracles had ceased.
Westminster Confession 1.1, repeated in the 1689 Baptist Confession: God's former ways of revealing his will are 'now ceased'.
Wesley argues the gifts faded through the church's decline, not God's withdrawal; the holiness movement's 'baptism with the Holy Spirit' prepares the ground for Pentecostalism.
Charles Parham's Topeka school and William Seymour's Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles launch modern Pentecostalism, with tongues as the initial evidence of Spirit baptism.
B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, ties the gifts to the apostles.
Charismatic renewal brings Pentecostal-style tongues, prophecy, and healing into mainline Protestant (Van Nuys, 1960) and Catholic (Duquesne, 1967) congregations.
The 'third wave' (Wimber's Vineyard; Grudem, Storms) brings the gifts into evangelical and some Reformed churches without the Pentecostal doctrine of a subsequent Spirit baptism.
Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views sets the cessationist (Gaffin), open-but-cautious (Saucy), and continuationist (Storms, Oss) cases side by side.

left: Fee, Paul, the Spirit, and the People of God

axes.name: Kingdom
bands: balanced on Israel and the church
axes.fair_summary: The one-people-of-God view holds that there is a single people of God across both testaments: in Christ, the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises to Abraham, and Christ's kingdom is present now; his return brings the new creation, for some after a millennial reign on earth. The dispensational view keeps Israel and the church distinct: God's promises to national Israel will be fulfilled literally in a future earthly kingdom, and most on this side expect the church to be caught up before a seven-year tribulation. Progressive dispensationalists add that Christ's kingdom has already begun, and many Pentecostals hold the rapture and the hope for Israel without the whole system.

history.what: Justin Martyr calls Christians 'the true spiritual Israel', yet he and Irenaeus expect a thousand-year reign of Christ on earth in a rebuilt Jerusalem.
Augustine, City of God, reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the present church age.
Augsburg Confession XVII condemns the teaching that the saints will possess an earthly kingdom before the resurrection of the dead.
Westminster Confession ch. 7: not two covenants of grace but one and the same, differently administered under law and gospel.
J. N. Darby, a leader of the Plymouth Brethren, teaches a distinct Israel and a pretribulational rapture.
Scofield Reference Bible carries dispensationalism into the pews.
Lewis Sperry Chafer founds Dallas Theological Seminary; his Systematic Theology (1947–48) and Ryrie's Dispensationalism Today (1965) give the system its classic form.
George Eldon Ladd's historic premillennialism: a future millennium, one people of God, the church through the tribulation.
Vatican II, Nostra Aetate: the Jews are not rejected by God (Romans 11:28–29); Presbyterian (1987) and Methodist (1996) statements add that the church has not replaced them.
Progressive dispensationalism (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) holds that the church already shares in the new covenant and kingdom blessings, while national Israel keeps a distinct future.

left: Ladd, The Gospel of the Kingdom

axes.name: Authority
axes.fair_summary: Those who read Scripture within the church's tradition hold that the creeds, the ecumenical councils, the consensus of the Fathers, and the church's living teaching (for Catholics, the teaching office of pope and bishops) are God's appointed means of guarding and interpreting his Word, and so carry real authority. Those who hold to Scripture alone may grant creeds and confessions real but subordinate authority, yet insist that only Scripture is infallible: any council may err, nothing may be required as an article of faith that cannot be proved from Scripture, and no council or teacher can bind the conscience against it.

history.what: Basil the Great, On the Holy Spirit 27: some of what the church holds comes from written teaching, some from the unwritten tradition of the apostles, and both have the same force.
Vincent of Lérins: hold what has been believed 'everywhere, always, by all.'
Second Council of Nicaea: 'we keep unchanged all the ecclesiastical traditions handed down to us, whether in writing or verbally.'
Luther at Worms: unless convinced by Scripture or clear reason he will not recant; his conscience is captive to the Word of God.
Council of Trent: the gospel is preserved in written books and in unwritten traditions.
Formula of Concord: Scripture is 'the only rule and norm' by which all teachers and teachings are judged; the ancient creeds are received as witnesses to it.
Westminster Confession ch. 1: Scripture is the supreme judge of all controversies, and councils may err.
Vatican II, Dei Verbum: Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine wellspring.

right: Mathison, The Shape of Sola Scriptura

axes.name: Worship
axes.fair_summary: Liturgical worship follows a set order and the church calendar, usually with the Eucharist at the center of the Lord's Day service, so that the whole congregation prays and sings with the historic church, in words tested over centuries, and joins the worship of heaven. Free worship holds that Scripture prescribes no fixed liturgy, so each congregation orders its own service around the Word read and preached, prayer, song, and the ordinances; some keep a plain, settled pattern and others leave the shape open for the Spirit to lead in the moment, with room for any member to contribute.

history.what: The Didache gives set Eucharistic prayers, while letting prophets give thanks as they wish.
Justin Martyr's First Apology 67: Sunday readings, a sermon, prayers, and the Eucharist, the presider giving thanks 'according to his ability'.
The eucharistic prayers of East and West take their lasting shape: the Liturgies of St Basil and St John Chrysostom, and the Roman Canon.
Zwingli's Zurich centers Sunday worship on sermon and prayer, without singing; Luther's German Mass keeps the Mass's order in German with congregational hymns.
Thomas Cranmer's first Book of Common Prayer gives the English church a single vernacular liturgy.

Puritans, following Calvin, hold that only what Scripture commands belongs in worship (the regulative principle); Hooker replies that the church may order what Scripture does not forbid; Westminster's Directory replaces the Prayer Book.
Charles Finney's revivalist 'new measures' reshape Protestant services.
Azusa Street revival under William Seymour: spontaneous singing, tongues and interpretation, and open testimony spread with Pentecostalism worldwide.

Vatican II, Sacrosanctum Concilium: reform of the Mass and the 'full, conscious, and active participation' of all the faithful; Anglican, Lutheran, and Presbyterian service books (1978–93) follow its lead.
Jesus movement and the contemporary worship movement (Calvary Chapel, Vineyard, Hillsong).

left: Ratzinger, The Spirit of the Liturgy

statements.text: God's choice of who will be saved is not based on anything he foresaw they would do.
A person whom God is drawing to salvation can still finally refuse him and be lost.
God alone works saving faith in a person; the sinner contributes nothing to conversion, not even the decision to believe.
In the Lord's Supper, Christ himself is given through the bread and wine, not only remembered.
Baptism is a public testimony to a faith already held, not a means by which God gives grace.
Infants should be baptized, not only those who profess faith for themselves.
The gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing are still given to the church today.
The miraculous gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament.
The Spirit still gives some Christians specific prophetic words for the church today.
God will yet give national Israel its promised land and kingdom on this earth.
There is one people of God across both testaments: the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises to Abraham.
The church is a new body begun at Pentecost, not the continuation of Old Testament Israel.
The early creeds and councils carry an authority of their own, not only as faithful summaries of what Scripture teaches.
Only Scripture is infallible; every creed, council, and teacher can err and must be tested by it.
When Christians disagree about a passage, the church's teaching office (bishops, councils, or a magisterium) has the final say.
Worship should follow a fixed written liturgy, with set prayers used week by week.
Each congregation should shape its own order of service rather than follow a prescribed liturgy.
The church year, with Advent, Lent, and Easter, should shape what a congregation reads, sings, and prays.

candidate_statements.text: Someone who has truly been born again can still fall away and be finally lost.
Whether a person comes to faith finally rests on their own free response to God's grace.
candidate_statements.note: A synergist item with no resistibility clause, so a four-item Grace axis can separate 'the sinner contributes nothing to conversion' from 'grace can be finally refused'. Keeping statement 2 as it stands is deliberate: it is the only item that separates the Lutheran entry (grace 33) from the Reformed entries (grace 5), so replacing it would collapse the pair that lutheran-4 and presbyterian-1 were about (lutheran-1, lutheran-2).

candidate_statements.text: God gives everyone enough grace to believe; the difference lies in how each person responds.
Whether a person believes is ultimately decided by God, not by the person.
In baptism God himself acts: he washes, seals, or joins the person to Christ.
The bread and wine remain ordinary bread and wine; the Supper's value is in remembering.
Christ's body and blood are received with the mouth by every communicant, believing or not.
With the Bible complete, the church no longer needs prophecy to hear from God.
Every Christian should eagerly seek the gifts of the Spirit, including the more dramatic ones.
Tongues today are learned or emotional speech, not the gift described in the New Testament.
The Old Testament land promises find their fulfilment in Christ and the new creation.
Ethnic Israel still has a distinct future role that the church has not taken over.
A Christian with an open Bible may rightly reject a teaching that every council has affirmed.
What the apostles handed down by word of mouth carries the same authority as what they wrote.
Practices not found in Scripture, however ancient, may be dropped by any church.
Spontaneous prayer in one's own words suits public worship better than prayers read from a book.
The congregation should say or sing set responses, creeds, and prayers together each week.
Worship should be able to change direction in the moment rather than follow an order fixed in advance.

changelog.before: Before anyone does anything, God has already chosen who will be saved, and his choice cannot fail.
changelog.after: God's choice of who will be saved is not based on anything he foresaw they would do.
changelog.why: Double-barreled, and both barrels are affirmed by synergists: Arminius, Wesley, the Orthodox (Dositheus, Decree 3) and the Southern Baptist Traditional Statement all hold an eternal, certain election grounded in foreknowledge, so the item did not discriminate monergism at all.

changelog.before: A person can genuinely resist God's grace and refuse salvation to the very end.
changelog.after: A person whom God is drawing to salvation can still finally refuse him and be lost.
changelog.why: As written a five-point Calvinist can honestly agree (WCF 10.4 and Dort III/IV: the non-elect resist the outward call to the end), so the item failed to separate the poles, and 'to the very end' read to Baptists as the perseverance question they answer the other way.

changelog.before: Saving faith is itself a gift God gives to those he has chosen, not the reason he chose them.
changelog.after: God alone works saving faith in a person; the sinner contributes nothing to conversion, not even the decision to believe.
changelog.why: The first clause is affirmed by Trent (Sess. VI ch. 8), Arminius, Wesley and Chrysostom alike, so only the subordinate clause discriminated and respondents had to guess which was keyed; with statement 1 now carrying election, statement 3 carries the monergism of conversion.

changelog.before: In the Lord's Supper, Christ is truly present in a way that goes beyond a symbol.
changelog.after: In the Lord's Supper, Christ himself is given through the bread and wine, not only remembered.
changelog.why: 'Truly present' was read by Mennonites, charismatics and Pentecostals of Christ present in the gathered congregation, so they were scored sacramental without holding a means-of-grace view; naming the elements locates the claim where the poles actually divide.

changelog.before: Baptism is an outward sign of a decision to follow Christ that has already been made.
changelog.after: Baptism is a public testimony to a faith already held, not a means by which God gives grace.
changelog.why: 'Outward sign' is the paedobaptist catechism definition of a sacrament and 'decision' is revivalist vocabulary that confessional credobaptists reject, so the item measured baptismal candidacy twice (with statement 6) and never asked the efficacy question the axis is named for.

changelog.before: The infants of believing parents should be baptized.
changelog.after: Infants should be baptized, not only those who profess faith for themselves.
changelog.why: 'The infants of believing parents' is verbatim Westminster covenant-household idiom (WCF 28.4); Rome, the East, Lutherans and the Prayer Book ground infant baptism differently.

changelog.before: Tongues, prophecy, and healing continue in the church today, as they did in Acts.
changelog.after: The gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing are still given to the church today.
changelog.why: 'As they did in Acts' added a restorationist claim about manner and scale that Anglicans, Catholics, Orthodox, Methodists and Reformed continuationists do not make, so non-cessationists were pushed toward the cessationist pole; naming them as gifts stops cessationists who pray for the sick from agreeing by accident.

changelog.before: The miraculous sign gifts ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament.
changelog.after: The miraculous gifts of tongues, prophecy, and healing ended with the apostles or the completion of the New Testament.
changelog.why: 'Sign gifts' is a category used only inside cessationist writing and rejected by the continuationists the page recommends, so the quiz's own voice asked one side to answer inside the other's frame; both grounds of cessation are kept.

changelog.before: A modern-day prophecy should be weighed carefully, but it can genuinely come from the Spirit.
changelog.after: The Spirit still gives some Christians specific prophetic words for the church today.
changelog.why: The item led with a concession every cessationist grants (test everything) and left 'prophecy' undefined, so a cessationist who allows Spirit-given impressions could agree and be scored continuationist.

changelog.before: God's promises to national Israel will be fulfilled literally in a future earthly kingdom.
changelog.after: God will yet give national Israel its promised land and kingdom on this earth.
changelog.why: 'Fulfilled literally' is Ryrie's sine qua non used as the neutral frame, so covenantal readers were told in the item that they do not read Scripture literally.

changelog.before: The church is the true Israel, heir to every promise God made to Abraham.
changelog.after: There is one people of God across both testaments: the church, Jew and Gentile together, inherits the promises to Abraham.
changelog.why: The axis's only left-keyed item was written as hard supersessionism, which Rome (Nostra Aetate 4), the Orthodox, the Church of England, PCUSA, ELCA and UMC have all formally disowned, so the least dispensational Christians in the world were pushed a third of an axis to the right for refusing a description they are on record against; the new wording is the fair summary's own and is what dispensationalism denies by definition.

changelog.before: Believers will be caught up to meet Christ before a seven-year tribulation.
changelog.after: The church is a new body begun at Pentecost, not the continuation of Old Testament Israel.
changelog.why: A third of the axis was spent on rapture timing, which Ryrie's own sine qua non exclude, so post-tribulational and pre-wrath dispensationalists were scored 67 and matched to 'Southern Baptist'; the replacement is the movement's actual distinctive.

changelog.before: The creeds and councils of the early church carry real authority, not just historical interest.
changelog.after: The early creeds and councils carry an authority of their own, not only as faithful summaries of what Scripture teaches.
changelog.why: 'Real authority' did not distinguish ministerial from magisterial authority, so every confessional Protestant agreed and was pushed toward the tradition pole; the new wording is denied by Article XXI, WCF 31, LBC 1.10 and the Formula's Rule and Norm, and affirmed by Rome and the East.

changelog.before: Every doctrine must be proven from Scripture alone; tradition can never bind the conscience.
changelog.after: Only Scripture is infallible; every creed, council, and teacher can err and must be tested by it.
changelog.why: Two claims the Anglican and Lutheran formularies answer differently (Article VI yes, Article XXXIV and FC X no), so the magisterial Reformation position collapsed to Unsure; infallibility is the line the poles actually divide on.

changelog.before: The church, not the individual reader, is the final interpreter of Scripture.
changelog.after: When Christians disagree about a passage, the church's teaching office (bishops, councils, or a magisterium) has the final say.
changelog.why: A false dichotomy in one side's apologetic vocabulary: magisterial Protestants deny both limbs (WCF 1.9-10), so they could not answer honestly, and Anabaptists and congregational Baptists read 'the church' as the gathered congregation and were scored toward Rome.

changelog.before: Worship should follow a set liturgy that connects us to the historic church.
changelog.after: Worship should follow a fixed written liturgy, with set prayers used week by week.
changelog.why: The rationale clause made disagreement read as disowning connection to the historic church, which Puritan, Reformed Baptist and Anabaptist congregations claim as strongly as anyone, and 'set liturgy' was ambiguous between a fixed order and a prayer book.

changelog.before: Worship should be free-form and led by the Spirit in the moment.
changelog.after: Each congregation should shape its own order of service rather than follow a prescribed liturgy.
changelog.why: The item measured spontaneity rather than non-liturgical worship and made disagreement feel like denying the Spirit, so the largest free-church families (Baptist, Bible church, Mennonite, Churches of Christ) had no honest answer and were pulled toward the liturgical pole, while liturgical charismatics were misplaced the other way.

changelog.before: Communion should be celebrated every week as the center of the service.
changelog.after: The church year, with Advent, Lent, and Easter, should shape what a congregation reads, sings, and prays.
changelog.why: Weekly communion is not a liturgical marker: it pushed Churches of Christ and the Plymouth Brethren, the freest congregations that exist, toward 'liturgical', and pushed Prayer Book Anglicans, whose rubric requires communion three times a year, toward 'free'. The church year tests set form and cross-loads on nothing.

disputed.proposed: Rename the right pole 'Scripture over tradition' and the top band 'Bible-only', because the 'Scripture alone' band was reachable only by respondents who deny the creeds any authority.
disputed.reason: The defect is real but it was caused by statements 13 and 15, not by the labels, and both have been rewritten. Under the revised items a Book of Concord or Westminster subscriber now scores 88-92 and reaches the top band, so the slogan is no longer handed only to biblicists. The proposed replacement would have created a new unfairness in its place: 'Bible-only' would be printed on Southern Baptist, Pentecostal, Bible-church and Restorationist respondents, who use 'sola scriptura' of themselves and would read Mathison's polemical coinage as a put-down. The half of the finding that survives on its own merits, bands[3] 'Scripture over tradition' (also asked for by catholic-23, presbyterian-10 and reformedcharismatic-9), has been applied.

disputed.proposed: Option (b): rename the poles 'Sacrament' and 'Ordinance' with bands ending 'ordinance-leaning', so that a 1689 Reformed Baptist at 67 is not told he is 'memorial-leaning'.
disputed.reason: Option (a) of the same blocker has been applied instead: statement 5 now tests whether God gives grace through baptism rather than who is baptized, so a 1689 subscriber scores 50 ('between sacramental and memorial') and the mis-score disappears without a rename. 'Memorial' also survives the holders'-own-vocabulary test that decided catholic-9: BF&M 2000 Art. VII says members 'memorialize the death of the Redeemer' and the AG Statement art. 6 calls the Supper 'a memorial'. 'Ordinance', by contrast, is used by both poles (LBC 30.7 calls the Supper 'that ordinance'; WLC 154 calls the sacraments ordinances), so it would name no pole.

disputed.proposed: Add a seventh axis (Church & World, or Church polity, or Church) or a seventh placement-only coordinate (the papacy; tongues as initial evidence) so that the peace churches, congregational polity, Rome versus Constantinople and Pentecostal versus charismatic are all measured.
disputed.reason: The demo is fixed at six axes and eighteen statements (apply.js warns on any other count, the page's radar has six spokes and the intro promises '18 statements, about 3 minutes'), and a coordinate the respondent answers but never sees on the compass is worse than an honest omission. What was applied instead: the Eastern Orthodox grace correction and the Catholic spirit correction (which widen the Rome/Constantinople gap from 13 to 18 units), the Pentecostal and charismatic coordinate changes (18.7 to 25.5 units), the 'peace church' qualifier on the Anabaptist entry, and a scope note under 'Nearest on the map' saying in the page's own voice that church government, the papacy and the peace-church convictions are not measured. The papacy and initial-evidence items are recommended for v1 in the report, where the item pool is being rebuilt anyway.

disputed.proposed: Rename the midpoint 'Neither agree nor disagree', add a sixth unscored 'Skip / don't know' option, score axes as 50 + 25 x mean over answered items, require a minimum number of answers per axis, and exclude unanswered axes from the headline and the distance.
disputed.reason: The harm this finding names, an all-Unsure respondent receiving a confident tradition match, is removed by two smaller changes that are applied: the tradition line is suppressed when all six axes sit within 10 of 50 (wesleyan-1), and the midpoint is relabelled 'Unsure / neither' (anabaptist-27). The rest is a scale redesign with per-axis minimums, an 'insufficient answers' state and a distance rescaled by sqrt(6/k), which cannot be expressed in this data file and is more instrument change than a three-minute demo needs. Recorded as a v1 recommendation.

disputed.reason: Correct and confirmed: agreeing with everything still yields 33/33/33/67/33/33 and the headline 'Monergist-leaning, sacramental-leaning, continuationist-leaning'. Eighteen balanced, opposite-keyed candidates are supplied in candidate_statements so the v1 expansion is a selection exercise rather than a redesign.

disputed.proposed: Restructure key_passages per axis as {left, right, both} and render three labelled rows, as read_more already does, so the promise that these are 'the passages each side reaches for' is visible rather than asserted.

The substance of the promise has been met inside the flat lists instead: every axis is now balanced pole by pole (Grace 3-3 with two read both ways, Gifts 3-3-1, Table and Authority 4-4, Kingdom 3-3-3), and the Kingdom list is ordered canonically so the chips do not group by side. Recommended for v1 in the report.

disputed.reason: The entry itself was removed. historian-1's own fix offers dropping the Newman line if length matters, and orthodox-19 asks for Basil and Second Nicaea in its place so the tradition pole is not three-quarters Roman with no Eastern source; Newman remains the first title in read_more.left, where the Orthodox objection to the development thesis costs nothing.

Calvary Chapel is added; Independent Baptist is not. disputed.proposed: Insert Calvin, Institutes II.10-11 (1559) as the one-covenant landmark alongside a reworded Westminster line.
disputed.reason: The 1646 line was reworded to state the one-covenant claim in Westminster's own words ('not two covenants of grace but one and the same'), which is what the finding's necessity fix asks for. Adding Calvin as well would give the left pole a fifth confessional entry against the right pole's four and duplicate a claim now stated in the entry immediately below it.

Only the broad-church note is applied. A third entry inside the already-tight Catholic/Orthodox/Anglican cluster would recreate the crowding that mockery-1 and survey-2 file as blockers, and the finding's own fairness and necessity verdicts recommend the note alone. An Anglo-Catholic respondent still sees 'Catholic (Roman and Eastern)' first, which the note now explains rather than leaving as a surprise.

disputed.proposed: Replace every straight apostrophe and quotation mark in the data and the HTML with typographic characters, on a page that already uses en dashes, middots, arrows and an ellipsis.
disputed.reason: Not applied. It is a global pass over strings that live in both the data file and the hand-written parts of the page, and the necessity lens dropped it as embarrassing nobody and mis-scoring nobody; doing it half-way (data only) would make the inconsistency more visible, not less. Worth one careful sweep at the v1 build, together with the other copy work listed in the report.
